content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler puffs, fruit are light airy bites specially formulated for children aged 6 months to 3 years. Made from whole grains and fruit purees, they contain no artificial colours, flavours or preservatives. The product dissolves easily in the mouth, reducing choking risk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The puffs are shaped like tiny clouds, making them visually appealing to toddlers.
Natural fruit purees (apple, pear, banana) provide sweetness without added sugar.
The snack is fortified with iron and vitamin C to support growth and immunity.
Each serving contains about 2 g of dietary fibre, promoting healthy digestion.
Packaging is made from recyclable material and features a convenient dispenser.

items.title: Supports growth
items.content: Iron and vitamin C help form haemoglobin and strengthen the immune system in young children.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The soft texture and lack of hard pieces make the puffs easy to chew and swallow for beginners of solid foods.

items.title: Contains dietary fibre
items.content: Fibre aids regular bowel movements and helps prevent constipation in toddlers.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Sweetness comes from natural fruit purees, avoiding refined sugar and supporting stable blood glucose levels.

items.title: Allergen‑free
items.content: The product is free from nuts, dairy and gluten, reducing the chance of allergic reactions.

items.title: Fruit allergy
items.content: Some children may be allergic to specific fruits (e.g., apple). Observe for any reaction when introducing the product.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Although designed to be safe, puffs should be given under adult supervision, especially to children under 12 months.

items.title: Iron content
items.content: Excess iron can cause gastrointestinal upset; follow the recommended serving size.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the puffs straight from the pack or add them to infant milk, yogurt or puree. If needed, lightly moisten them to make swallowing easier.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a cool, dry place with the package tightly sealed. Once opened, use within 4–6 weeks to maintain crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Cereal is a ready‑to‑eat breakfast made from processed grains (wheat, corn, rice, oats, etc.), often fortified with vitamins and minerals. It is typically served with milk or yogurt and may contain dried fruit, nuts, sweeteners, and flavorings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial dry breakfast cereal was created in 1863 by the Jones Company.
There are more than 200 varieties of ready‑to‑eat cereals, differing in flavor and composition.
Most brands add iron and B‑vitamins to compensate for nutrient losses during grain processing.
Some options contain whole grains, which retain more fiber than fully refined cereals.
Dry cereals often use a “puffing” process where grain is heated under pressure, creating a light, porous texture.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Cereals provide quick and sustained energy through easily digestible carbs.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2, B6 and folate support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Fortified cereals help prevent iron deficiency, especially in children and women of reproductive age.

items.title: Fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain varieties supply dietary fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Most dry cereals have a low fat content, making them suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Many varieties contain added sugars, which can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of cavities.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Common ingredients include nuts, soy, or dairy, which may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Low protein
items.content: Compared with whole grains, most cereals provide relatively little protein.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Most cereals are wheat‑based and unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour milk, kefir, or a plant‑based beverage over the cereal and let it sit for 2–3 minutes. Add fresh berries, banana slices, nuts, or honey to enhance flavor and nutritional value.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the package in a cool, dry place and reseal tightly after each use. For long‑term storage, transfer to an airtight container to prevent moisture absorption.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned cherries (Cerasus) are whole cherries that have been blanched, pitted and packed in syrup or their own juice. They retain a sweet‑tart flavor, bright aroma and most of their nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cherries belong to the Rosaceae family and are close relatives of sweet cherries and plums.
Canning allows cherries to be stored for 2‑3 years without loss of taste.
Cherries are rich in antioxidants, especially anthocyanins, which give them their deep red color.
Traditional canning uses a sugar syrup, but sugar‑free versions also exist.
Canned cherries are commonly used in baking, desserts and sauces.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Anthocyanins and vitamin C help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Flavonoids in cherries may improve circulation and lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium aids in blood pressure regulation and muscle function.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber promotes healthy bowel movements.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Canned cherries are low in fat and moderately caloric, making them suitable for weight‑conscious diets.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Most canned cherries contain added sugar, which may be unsuitable for diabetics or those watching their sugar intake.

items.title: Cherry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cherries.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain brands may use preservatives such as sodium sorbate.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidic nature can irritate a sensitive stomach.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned cherries can be enjoyed straight from the jar, added to yogurt, oatmeal, salads, baked goods, sauces, and smoothies. They pair well with cottage cheese, ice cream and chocolate.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened jars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 5‑7 days. Discard if mold, off‑odor, or other signs of spoilage appear.

content.title: About
content.content: Pompano (Trachinotus ovatus) is a marine fish from the jack family, found in warm coastal waters of the Indo‑Pacific region. The fillet is high in protein, contains beneficial omega‑3 fatty acids, and has a delicate, slightly sweet flavor. Baking or broiling preserves its natural aroma and yields a tender, juicy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pompano is often called the “golden fish” because of its bright golden coloration.
The species grows quickly, reaching up to 30 cm in length within its first year.
Culinary chefs value pompano for its tender flesh that separates easily from the bone.
In Japan, pompano is served as sushi and sashimi, while in the United States it is popular as herb‑roasted fillets.
Pompano can be farm‑raised, making it a more sustainable and accessible seafood option.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Pompano fillet provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: The fish contains EPA and DHA, which promote heart and brain health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Pompano supplies B12, B6, and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It is a good source of selenium, phosphorus, and potassium, which aid immune function and bone health.

items.title: Low mercury levels
items.content: Compared with larger predatory fish, pompano typically has low mercury, making it safe for regular consumption.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to seafood, including pompano.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: As with any marine fish, pompano can contain trace pollutants (e.g., PCBs); choose reputable suppliers.

items.title: Digestive comfort
items.content: Eating large portions at once may cause heaviness for people with sensitive digestion.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Season the fillet with olive oil, salt, and herbs (rosemary, thyme) and bake at 180 °C for 12‑15 minutes. For broiling, lightly coat with a thin breadcrumb crust and cook 3‑4 minutes per side until golden. Serve with lemon wedges, fresh vegetables, or a light yogurt‑based sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh pompano fillets refrigerated at 0‑2 °C, wrapped in plastic film or in an airtight container, and use within 2 days. Frozen fillets can be stored up to 3 months at –18 °C; thaw in the refrigerator before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Fritter is a small fried dough snack made from wheat flour, eggs, milk and a touch of sugar. It has a golden crust and a soft, slightly airy interior. Fritters are often served as a quick snack or a breakfast side.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The tradition of making fritters dates back to medieval Europe, where they were cooked over an open fire.
There are many variations: sweet versions with berries, fruit or chocolate and savory ones with cheese, herbs or meat.
In the United States, apple fritters – dough pieces with apple chunks and cinnamon – are especially popular.
Fritters are commonly prepared at home on a skillet, but they can also be baked to reduce fat content.
In Japan, a similar concept exists in the form of okonomiyaki, cooked on a special griddle.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The carbohydrates from flour and sugar provide a quick source of energy.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Eggs add a modest amount of complete protein.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Flour and eggs supply B1, B2 and B6 vitamins important for metabolism.

items.title: Calcium
items.content: Milk contributes calcium, beneficial for bone health.

items.title: Easily digestible carbs
items.content: Simple carbs in fritters are rapidly absorbed, useful before physical activity.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: When fried, fritters absorb oil, making them calorie‑dense.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional recipes use wheat flour, which can be problematic for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet versions may raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Fried foods can cause stomach upset in individuals with sensitive digestion.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve fritters warm, lightly dusted with powdered sugar, or drizzled with honey or maple syrup. They also pair well with fruit sauces, sour cream, or cream cheese. For a healthier twist, bake them and serve with berry purée.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked fritters in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, refrigerate them for up to 5 days or freeze in a zip‑lock bag for up to 2 months. Reheat in the oven before serving to restore crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Mayonnaise-type salad dressing is an emulsion of vegetable oil, eggs, vinegar or lemon juice, and seasonings. It has a creamy texture, mild flavor, and is used as a salad dressing, sandwich spread, and base for many other sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The classic mayonnaise was created in the 19th century in France, and similar emulsions have spread worldwide.
Egg yolks act as natural emulsifiers, binding oil and water together.
There are many variations: olive‑oil based, yogurt‑based, avocado‑based, and other plant‑based versions.
Mayonnaise-type dressing is often taught in culinary schools to demonstrate emulsion techniques.
In many countries it is considered a “universal sauce” and is found in almost every household fridge.

items.title: Source of healthy fats
items.content: When made with oils high in monounsaturated fats (e.g., olive oil), the dressing can help maintain healthy cholesterol levels.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs provide vitamin B12, riboflavin, and biotin, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Contains vitamin E
items.content: The oil component supplies vitamin E, an antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Improves nutrient absorption
items.content: Fats aid the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) from other foods in the salad.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: Provides calories that can be useful for people with high energy needs, such as athletes.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: The presence of eggs makes the dressing a potential allergen for individuals with egg allergy.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Because of the oil, the dressing is calorie‑dense and should be used in moderation.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Raw eggs may contain Salmonella; using pasteurized eggs or commercially prepared products reduces this risk.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain cholesterol, which may be a concern for people with hypercholesterolemia.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use as a dressing for green or vegetable salads, as a spread for sandwiches, in dips for veggie sticks, or as a base for more complex sauces (e.g., with mustard or herbs).

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C in a sealed container. Once opened, it is usually good for 1–2 weeks. Discard if it develops off‑odors, color changes, or mold.

content.title: About
content.content: Roll wheat (cracked wheat) is whole wheat kernels that have been coarsely broken into small pieces. The product retains most of the grain’s nutrients, offers a mild nutty flavor and a slightly chewy texture. It is used as a side dish, in salads, soups, pilafs and baked goods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cracked wheat is a staple in many Eastern European and Mediterranean cuisines.
Compared with whole wheat berries, cracked wheat absorbs water faster, reducing cooking time.
Wheat has been cultivated for over 10,000 years, making it one of the oldest crops.
Roll wheat can be made from whole grain or from refined kernels, affecting fiber content.
In some regions the product is called “bulgur,” although bulgur is usually par‑boiled after cracking.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Cracked wheat provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies thiamine, niacin and folate, which are essential for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Wheat delivers magnesium, phosphorus, iron and zinc, contributing to bone health and immune function.

items.title: Lower glycemic impact after soaking
items.content: Pre‑soaking and thorough cooking lower the glycemic index, making it more suitable for people monitoring glucose.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Phenolic compounds in wheat help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to wheat proteins.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: The product is unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Possible contamination
items.content: Improper storage can lead to mold growth and mycotoxin formation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cracked wheat can be boiled in water or broth until tender (about 15‑20 minutes), added to salads, used as a base for vegetarian patties, mixed into soups, or cooked as a porridge with fruit and nuts. Soaking for 2‑4 hours before cooking speeds up the process.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct light. For longer shelf life keep it in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent mold. Typical shelf life is up to 12 months; discard if a stale or sour odor develops.
